intro.caption: Lesson 6-11 — solving fraction division word problems. The mission map splits at every turn. One tunnel is for problems that ask HOW MANY GROUPS fit. The other is for problems that ask HOW MUCH is in ONE group. Pick the right tunnel at three gates and a boss to reach the exit.

balloons.t: Every fork asks one thing: how many groups, or how much in one group?
Pick wrong and you take the scenic route. The scenic route has bats.
Left, right, who cares? Division is division. That's classified.
It matters. First find what you KNOW: the size of each group, or the number of groups.

pages.caption: If you know the size of each group, you are finding how many groups. If you know how many groups (or what part of one group you have), you are finding how much in one group.

balloons.t: Cyan tunnel: how many groups. Yellow tunnel: how much in one group.
Read the problem. Then pick. In that order, Teo.
The total is the dividend. It goes first. The other number is the divisor.
⅗ liter only fills ⅓ of my tank. The whole tank is the mystery.
Solve it. Then multiply back to check. Then ask: is it reasonable?
½ ÷ ¼ = ⅛. Small numbers, small answer. Classified.
Last fork. My squad picked a tunnel in one second. Without reading.
That explains the bats in your hair.
Right tunnel every time. Zero bats. I am almost disappointed.

win.caption: Ask what you know. Know the size of each group? Find how many groups. Know the number of groups, or what part of a group you have? Find how much is in one group. Write total ÷ divisor, solve, and check by multiplying.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Choose the Tunnel
gates.prompt: For each problem, choose the tunnel: is it asking how many groups or how much in one group?
hints: Conceptual: look at what the problem tells you. A known size for each group means you count groups. A known number of groups, or a part of one group, means you find one group's amount.
Procedural: underline the total. Then circle the other number. Is it the size of one group, or how many groups (or what part of a group)?

steps: Practice A: ⅝ liter of juice poured into ⅛-liter cups. We know each cup's size, so we find HOW MANY GROUPS: ⅝ ÷ ⅛ = 5 cups.
Practice B: 2 agents share ⅖ liter. We know there are 2 groups, so we find HOW MUCH IN ONE GROUP: ⅖ ÷ 2 = ⅕ liter.
Same operation, different question. Read first, then pick.
worked.q: Two agents share ⅔ meter of tape. Which question is it?

items.q: Farah has ¾ liter of water. Each cup holds ⅛ liter. How many cups can she fill?

options.t: How much in one group (yellow tunnel)
options.fb: Wrong tunnel. You already know one cup's size, ⅛ liter. You are counting how many cups fit.
Dead end. The total, ¾ liter, is already given. Multiplying would make a new total.

items.q: ⅔ kg of rations fills ½ of a pack. How much fills a whole pack?

options.fb: Wrong tunnel. You are not counting packs. You know what PART of one pack the ⅔ kg fills.
Dead end. Multiplying ⅔ × ½ gives a smaller amount, but a whole pack holds more than half a pack.

options.t: How much in one group (yellow tunnel)

items.q: 3 agents share ¾ meter of rope equally. How much does each agent get?

options.fb: Dead end. ¾ × 3 would be more rope than the team has. Sharing makes each part smaller.

options.t: How much in one group (yellow tunnel)

options.fb: Wrong tunnel. You already know there are 3 groups: the agents. You want one agent's share.

gates.pass: Cyan, yellow, yellow. Three right tunnels. Teo took the left one anyway and came back with a bat on his head.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Write the Equation
gates.prompt: Write the division equation for each problem. The total is the dividend and goes first.
hints: Conceptual: the total is what gets split. It comes first. The number you divide by is the size of a group, the number of groups, or the part of a group.
Procedural: write total ÷ divisor = unknown. Then solve by multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor.

steps: Practice: ⅘ meter of wire is cut into ⅕-meter pieces. How many pieces, p?
The total ⅘ is the dividend. The piece size ⅕ is the divisor: ⅘ ÷ ⅕ = p.
worked.q: ⅔ liter fills ½ of a bottle. Write the equation for a whole bottle, b.

items.q: A ¾ km trail is split into sections that are each ⅜ km long. Which equation finds the number of sections, s?

options.fb: The order is flipped. The trail, ¾ km, is the total, so it goes first.
Multiplying finds a part OF the trail. You want how many ⅜-km sections fit.
Subtracting finds one leftover distance, not a count of sections.

items.label: ¾ ÷ ⅜ = s. b =
items.aria: number of sections on the trail

fb.msg: That's ¾ × ⅜. Multiply by the reciprocal instead: ¾ × 8/3.
That's ⅜ ÷ ¾, the order flipped. How many ⅜s fit in ¾?

items.fbDefault: Write ¾ as eighths: 6/8. How many 3/8s fit in 6/8?

items.q: ⅗ liter of fuel fills ⅓ of Ozzie's tank. Which equation finds a full tank, t?

options.fb: That's a third OF the fuel. A full tank holds MORE than ⅗ liter, not less.
The order is flipped. The fuel, ⅗ liter, is the total you have, so it goes first.
Adding mixes liters with a part of the tank. Divide the fuel by the part it fills.

gates.pass: Two sections, and the tank equation is ⅗ ÷ ⅓ = t. The map lights the next tunnel.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Does It Make Sense?
gates.prompt: Solve Ozzie's tank problem, ⅗ ÷ ⅓ = t. Then check the answer and judge Teo's.
hints: Conceptual: multiplication and division are inverse operations. If ⅗ ÷ ⅓ = t, then t × ⅓ must equal ⅗.
Procedural: multiply ⅗ by the reciprocal of ⅓, which is 3. Then multiply your answer by ⅓ and see if you get ⅗.

steps: Practice: ⅔ liter fills ½ of a bottle. ⅔ ÷ ½ = ⅔ × 2 = 4/3 = 1 ⅓ liters.
Check: 1 ⅓ × ½ = 4/3 × 1/2 = 4/6 = ⅔. It matches.
Reasonable? ⅔ fills only half, so the whole bottle must hold more than ⅔. 1 ⅓ is more. Yes.

items.label: ⅗ ÷ ⅓ = t. t =

fb.msg: That's ⅗ × ⅓. A full tank must hold MORE than the ⅗ liter that fills just a third.
That's ⅓ ÷ ⅗, the order flipped. The fuel, ⅗, is divided.
⅗ fills only one third. The whole tank is three thirds.

items.fbDefault: Multiply ⅗ by 3, the reciprocal of ⅓. Write the answer as a mixed number.

options.fb: That does not use your answer at all. Multiply the answer by the divisor.
Multiply by the divisor, ⅓, not by the total. And 1 ⅘ × ⅗ is 27/25, not ⅓.
Adding never undoes division. The inverse of dividing is multiplying.

items.q: Teo says ½ ÷ ¼ = ⅛. Is his answer reasonable?

options.t: Yes. Small numbers make a small answer.
options.fb: Size is not the test. Ask how many ¼s fit in ½. Two of them do.
⅛ × ¼ = 1/32, not ½. His answer fails the check.

options.t: No. Two ¼s fit in ½, so the answer is 2.

gates.pass: 1 ⅘ liters, and 1 ⅘ × ⅓ = ⅗. Teo's ⅛ was really ½ × ¼. He calls that one "a decoy."

gates.title: Boss Gate · The Rope Bridge
gates.prompt: Last fork. Choose the tunnel, solve, and earn the bridge code.
hints: Conceptual: for each problem, decide first: do you know the size of a group, or the number of groups?
Procedural: write total ÷ divisor. Multiply by the reciprocal. Check by multiplying the answer by the divisor.

steps: Practice: 4 agents share ⅔ kg of chalk. We know the number of groups, so we find how much in one group.
⅔ ÷ 4 = ⅔ × ¼ = 2/12 = ⅙ kg each.
worked.q: How many ¼-meter pieces can be cut from 3 meters?

items.q: 3 agents share ⅞ kg of climbing chalk equally. Which tunnel?

options.fb: Wrong tunnel. You already know there are 3 groups. You want one agent's share.

options.t: How much in one group (yellow tunnel)

options.fb: Dead end. ⅞ × 3 is more chalk than the bag holds. Sharing makes each part smaller.

items.label: ⅞ ÷ 3 = kg for each agent:
items.aria: kilograms of chalk for each agent

fb.msg: That's ⅞ × 3, more than the whole bag. Sharing makes each part smaller than ⅞.
That's 3 ÷ ⅞, the order flipped. The chalk is what gets shared.
⅞ kg is the whole bag. One agent gets only a third of it.

items.fbDefault: Multiply ⅞ by ⅓, the reciprocal of 3.

items.label: Bridge code · 2 m of rope cut into ⅖-m ties. Ties:
items.aria: number of two fifths meter rope ties

fb.msg: That's 2 × ⅖. You know each tie's size, so count how many ties fit.
1 is 2 ÷ 2. It ignores the fifths. Multiply 2 by 5/2.
10 is 2 ÷ ⅕. Each tie is TWO fifths, so half as many fit.

items.fbDefault: Multiply 2 by the reciprocal of ⅖, which is 5/2.

gates.pass: 7/24 kg each, and the bridge code is 5. The bridge locks into place. Vale's squad is still in the bat tunnel.

journal.heading: Lesson 6-11 — what the mission map taught us
rows: You know the size of each group. ¾ liter ÷ ⅛ liter per cup counts the cups.
You know the number of groups, or the part of a group. ⅞ kg ÷ 3 agents = 7/24 kg each. ⅗ L ÷ ⅓ of a tank = 1 ⅘ L in a full tank.
Total ÷ divisor = unknown. The total goes first: ¾ ÷ ⅜ = s, so s = 2.
Multiplying undoes dividing: 1 ⅘ × ⅓ = ⅗. Then ask if the answer is reasonable.
Picking a tunnel without reading. ½ ÷ ¼ asks how many ¼s fit in ½. The answer is 2, not ⅛.
journal.quote: "Read the problem, then pick the tunnel. Or pick first and meet the bats." — Chip

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 6-11 (Fraction Division Problem Solving) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: deciding whether a word problem asks how many groups or how much in one group, writing total ÷ divisor equations, solving, and checking for reasonableness with inverse operations.
standards: Interpret and compute quotients of fractions; solve word problems involving division of fractions
